subtype: Approach: working backward from the fair date [Thinking]
passage:
"Sudha Masi, the science fair is on the twenty-first. That's three weeks."
"Plenty of time, then."
"No, listen. Start from the end. What do I need on the last day?"
"Your board, I suppose."
"Right. The display board takes a whole week, with the chart and photos. So week three is the board."
"And before that?"
"The plants need time to grow. That's week two, the experiment."
"Then week one?"
"Buying pots and seeds and setting up. So I start this Saturday, not next month."
Sudha laughed. "You planned it backwards."
"It's the only way I knew when to start."
Sunaina drew three boxes on the calendar and wrote BOARD in the last one in her neatest letters.

subtype: Approach: working backward from the fair date [Thinking]

subtype: Approach: writing observations in a daily notebook [Action]

"Raghav, why are you on the balcony at six?"
"Measuring, Salma didi."
"Measuring what?"
"My bean plant. Every morning, same time, same ruler."
She peered at his notebook. Rows of dates. 3rd: 2 cm. 4th: 2.5 cm. 5th: 3.5 cm.
"Why write it all down? You can just see it's growing."
"Seeing isn't numbers. At the fair they'll ask how much it grew, and when. If I don't write it, I'll be guessing."
"Why the same time?"
"So it's fair. Plants grow more in some hours."
On fair day, Raghav's line graph went up in neat steps, and every point had a date under it.

qa.a: Salma first thinks it is unnecessary, then starts to see why dates and numbers matter when he explains.

subtype: Approach: writing observations in a daily notebook [Action]
passage: For the science fair I grew a tomato seedling in a yoghurt cup on our windowsill. Every morning, before brushing my teeth, I held a ruler against the stem and wrote the height and the date in a small blue notebook. Some days it was boring. Some days it didn't grow at all, and I wrote 0 anyway. My friend Gautam said, "Bhai, just draw the graph on the last day." But at the end I didn't have to remember anything. I had twenty-one numbers with dates. When the judge asked when it grew fastest, I opened the notebook: days nine to twelve. She nodded and wrote something down. I think I, Raghav, grew a bit too.

subtype: Approach: getting a parent to do the main work [Pitfall]
passage: At our school science fair, my table was right next to Jeevan's. His model of a water filter was the best-looking in the hall: clear pipes, three layers of sand and stones, a tap that really dripped. I heard someone say his father had built it over the weekend while Jeevan watched cartoons. The report was typed and printed. When the judge came, she asked, "Why is the charcoal layer in the middle?" Jeevan looked at the model. "Because... it looks nice there?" She asked what the sand did. He said, "Cleans it." "How?" He didn't answer. The judge moved on to me. Jeevan stared at his shoes. I'm not sure what he felt, but he didn't look proud of the beautiful model.

qa.a: It was a model of a water filter.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have been feeling when he stared at his shoes?

qa.q: How might the day look to Jeevan's father?
qa.a: If he hears about the judge's questions, the father might realise that doing the work himself meant Jeevan learned little.

grounding: It shows a child who let his father build the model and write the report, and then could not answer the judge's questions.

subtype: Approach: getting a parent to do the main work [Pitfall]

subtype: Approach: repeating the experiment when the result looks odd [Revision]
passage: In the school science lab, Kavitha's two bean plants had been growing for ten days, one on the windowsill and one in the dark cupboard. On Monday she opened the cupboard and frowned. The dark plant was almost as tall and green as the window one. That wasn't what she'd read. Parul ma'am came over. "Hmm. What's different from the plan?" Kavitha looked at the cupboard. The door had a gap. And the lab assistant often left it open in the mornings to get beakers. "It wasn't dark," she said. "Not really." That afternoon she planted two new cups, taped the cupboard door shut and put a sign on it. Ten days later the result was clear: the dark plant was tall, thin and yellow.

qa.q: How many days had the plants been growing on Monday?
qa.a: They had been growing for ten days.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when she saw the dark plant was nearly as green?
qa.a: She felt puzzled and a bit let down, because it did not match what she had read.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha do to make sure the new test is fair?
qa.a: She could check the cupboard each day and note that it stayed shut, so she can show the dark was really dark.

qa.q: How does the repeated test look to Parul ma'am?
qa.a: Parul ma'am sees a student who noticed an odd result and fixed the cause, which is the kind of thinking a teacher hopes for.

grounding: It shows a girl whose dark-cupboard plant grew too well, realising the door had been open and repeating the test with it shut for a clearer result.

subtype: Approach: repeating the experiment when the result looks odd [Revision]
passage: I share a room with my sister Neelam, and her science project lived in our cupboard for two weeks: one bean plant in a cup, meant to be in the dark. On Saturday she took it out and looked confused. "It's too green. It's supposed to be pale." I didn't say anything. I had been leaving the cupboard door open to take my shirts out every morning, and I had not closed it once. When I told her, she didn't shout. She just sat on the bed for a minute, then planted a new cup. She taped a note on the cupboard: KEEP SHUT. SCIENCE. Our neighbour Lokesh uncle lent her a black cloth to cover the gap. Twelve days later the new plant was pale and stretched.

qa.a: She taped a note saying KEEP SHUT. SCIENCE.

qa.q: What else could Neelam do to protect the test this time?

qa.q: How does the problem look to the sibling who left the door open?
qa.a: The sibling feels guilty for spoiling the test and is relieved when Neelam doesn't shout.

grounding: It shows a girl whose dark plant grew too well, finding the cupboard had been open, and repeating the test with it shut for a clearer result.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]
passage: In the small school at Wai, the science exhibition was on Saturday, and Dhruv's project was about how rainwater can be collected from roofs. He knew the model by heart, but when he tried to explain it to his mother, he rambled for five minutes. So he made a rule: one minute, three parts. What I wondered. What I did. What I found. He practised in the courtyard, timing himself with the kitchen clock. Then he asked his sister Esha to be a difficult judge. "Why a roof and not the ground?" "What if it doesn't rain?" "Is the water safe to drink?" He stumbled on that last one, so they worked out an honest answer together: "Not without cleaning." On Saturday, the real judge asked exactly that.

subtype: Approach: rehearsing how to explain the project to visitors [Action]

subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]
passage: The morning of the science fair, the bus broke down, and Lalremsiami arrived twenty minutes late with her two bean plants wobbling in a box. Her prediction had been that the cupboard plant would not grow at all. It had grown, long and thin, but it was pale yellow. On the bus she had thought about hiding it and showing only the window plant. Or saying it was green in real life. But when Santosh sir, the judge, stopped at her table, she put both plants in front of him. "I thought this one wouldn't grow. It did. But it's pale. That surprised me. I want to find out why." Santosh sir leaned closer. "That's the most interesting thing I've heard today."

subtype: Approach: presenting an unexpected result honestly [Revision]

subtype: Approach: getting used to water in the shallow end first [Thinking]
passage: Vidya, beti, you don't want to go to swimming class because the water scares you? Sit. Your Nilesh Dada was the same. We lived by a river, and every boy in the village could swim except me. They'd dive off the rock, and I'd sit on the bank. One day my uncle said, "Don't start with the rock. Start where the water is at your knees." So I did. I stood in the shallows and splashed, day after day, until my heart stopped jumping. I told myself: if I feel safe here, I'll go to my waist. Then I did. Then I learnt to float with him holding me. I never dived off that rock, beti. But I swam, and he was always nearby.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's uncle have seen the slow progress?
qa.a: The uncle likely felt patient and proud, watching the boy grow braver step by step while staying nearby.

grounding: An elder recalls being a boy afraid of water, starting in the shallows until he felt safe and then moving on to floating.

On day five: "Lie back on the noodle. I'm right here." She lay back on the foam tube and looked at the sky. Nothing bad happened. "One thing at a time," the coach said. At home she told her mother, "It's like stairs. I only climb one step a day."

subtype: Approach: following the coach's step-by-step drills [Action]

passage: At the sports club pool, the beginners had to stay in the shallow end until the coach said otherwise. The water closed over his head, and he couldn't find the bottom or the top. He thrashed, swallowed water. Rekha, the lifeguard, was already in the water. She hooked him under the arms and pulled him to the side. He clung to the edge, coughing, shaking. When the coach arrived, he sat with Varun on the bench. "Brave is doing it when you're ready, with me here," he said. Varun nodded, still shaking.

subtype: Approach: jumping into the deep end to prove he is brave [Pitfall]

The coach had gone to the office for a minute, and one of the older boys dared him. Francis looked at the water for a long time. Then he jumped. He didn't come up properly. His arms were slapping the water and his face kept going under. I yelled for help, and the lifeguard dived in and pulled him out. The coach ran back. Francis sat wrapped in a towel, very quiet. The coach talked to him for a long time, and then called his mother. I don't know if he was more scared or more embarrassed. Probably both.

passage: At the local pool in Toronto, Xin tried to float on her back six times, and six times her legs sank like stones. "I'm too heavy," she said, spluttering. Coach Chidi crouched at the edge. "You're not heavy. You're tight. Look at your hands." Her fists were clenched. Her shoulders were up by her ears. "Try this. Big slow breath in. Let your arms go floppy, like seaweed." Xin breathed in, let her fingers open and her arms drift out. She leaned back. The water came up round her ears. Her legs sank a little, then rose. She stayed there, looking at the ceiling, and heard the coach laugh softly. "That's it. The water's holding you."
